content.title: About
content.content: Acerola cherries (Malpighia emarginata) are small, bright red fruits native to the Caribbean, Central America, and northern South America. They look like cherries but are not related to them, and have a tart, slightly sweet flavor with thin, juicy flesh. Acerola is best known as one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C and is usually sold as juice, puree, or powder.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Acerola is often called Barbados cherry or West Indian cherry, but it is not a true cherry.
It has one of the highest vitamin C contents of any fruit, many times higher than oranges by weight.
Acerola fruits are very perishable and begin to lose vitamin C soon after harvest.
Because of this, acerola is usually processed quickly into juice, puree, or frozen products.
The fruit is popular in Brazil and across the tropics.

items.title: Extremely rich in vitamin C
items.content: Acerola is an outstanding source of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains carotenoids
items.content: Acerola provides carotenoids, some of which the body can convert into vitamin A.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Anthocyanins and other polyphenols have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Easy to use as powder or juice
items.content: Acerola powder and juice can be added to smoothies and drinks.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Acerola is tart and acidic and may bother sensitive stomachs or tooth enamel.

items.title: Too much vitamin C
items.content: Very high intakes of vitamin C may cause diarrhea and stomach upset and may contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

items.title: Iron overload conditions
items.content: Vitamin C increases iron absorption, so people with iron overload conditions should consult a healthcare professional.

items.title: Added sugar and allergies
items.content: Sweetened acerola products can contain added sugar, and allergies are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh acerola can be eaten whole, with the seeds, but it is rarely available outside tropical regions. Acerola juice, puree, and powder can be added to smoothies, drinks, yogurt, and desserts, and the fruit is used in jams and ice cream. Follow product labels for amounts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh acerola cherries are very perishable and should be refrigerated and used within a day or two, or frozen. Keep acerola powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Refrigerate juice after opening.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-tomatoe.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables, no fat added

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach, broccoli or kale) prepared without added oil or fat. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while the vegetables supply vitamins, minerals and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are often called a “complete” food because they contain all essential amino acids.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant whose availability increases with cooking.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables contain chlorophyll, which may support the body’s detoxification processes.
Cooking without fat reduces the calorie count while preserving most nutrients.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One serving provides about 6 g of protein, important for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12, riboflavin and folate, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Lycopene and carotenoids
items.content: Tomatoes deliver lycopene and beta‑carotene, antioxidants that benefit skin and eye health.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients
items.content: Dark‑green vegetables add dietary fiber, vitamin K, magnesium and iron, which support bone and blood health.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Without added fat the dish is relatively light, roughly 150–180 kcal per serving.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the vegetables are not organic, pesticide residues may be present; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in diced tomatoes and finely chopped dark‑green vegetables. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated non‑stick pan and cook over medium heat, stirring gently until the eggs set. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat in a pan without adding oil.

fish-and-vegetables-excluding-carrots-br.title: Fish and Vegetables without Carrots, Broccoli, Dark‑Green Leafy Greens

content.title: About
content.content: A combination of tender fish (such as salmon, cod, or hake) with a variety of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens and potatoes, creates a light, nutrient‑dense dish rich in protein, vitamins, and minerals. Preparing it without soy sauce makes it suitable for those avoiding soy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fish is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart and brain health.
Vegetables like zucchini, bell pepper, tomatoes, and cauliflower provide antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.
Excluding potatoes lowers the dish’s glycemic index, making it more suitable for blood‑sugar control.
Steaming preserves most of the vitamins and minerals in both fish and vegetables.
Fish‑and‑vegetable dishes are staples in Mediterranean diets, known for their health benefits.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish supplies complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: These polyunsaturated fats reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Fish and vegetables contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iodine, selenium, magnesium, and potassium, which aid thyroid function, immunity, and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Omitting potatoes and starchy vegetables makes the meal suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species can contain mercury or other toxins; choosing smaller species and reputable sources is advisable.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: If the dish is heavily salted or uses ready‑made seasonings, sodium intake can become too high, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Improper storage
items.content: Fresh fish‑vegetable dishes spoil quickly at room temperature; keep refrigerated and consume within 1‑2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish can be served hot, baked, or steamed. Cut fish into bite‑size pieces and vegetables into large cubes, then bake together with a drizzle of olive oil and herbs (such as thyme or rosemary). Serve with lemon wedges or a light yogurt‑based sauce without soy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven or a steamer before serving. Do not freeze fish together with vegetables for long‑term storage, as texture may deteriorate.

content.title: About
content.content: Grapes are the edible berries of the grapevine (Vitis vinifera), cultivated in temperate regions worldwide. Raw grapes have a sweet‑tart flavor and a juicy, crisp texture. They are eaten fresh, added to salads, desserts, juices, and used in winemaking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grapes are one of the oldest cultivated plants, with cultivation dating back over 8,000 years.
There are more than 8,000 grape varieties, differing in color, taste, and berry size.
Grape seeds contain polyphenols that have antioxidant properties.
Vineyards can live over a hundred years; some ancient vines in Europe are considered cultural heritage.
Grapes were called the “fruit of the gods” in ancient Greek and Roman mythology.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Grapes contain resveratrol, quercetin, and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Flavonoids in grapes improve vascular function and may lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber in the skin and pulp promotes healthy digestion and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals enhance the immune system.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to grapes, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fresh grapes are high in natural sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Unwashed grapes may carry pesticide residues; it is recommended to rinse them thoroughly before eating.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidity of grapes can irritate the stomach in those sensitive to acidic foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat grapes raw as a snack, add them to salads, yogurts, cereals, use in desserts and smoothies. They can be frozen for sorbets or incorporated into sauces. Both skin‑on and skin‑off grapes are nutritious.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store grapes in the refrigerator in their original bag or a perforated container to allow airflow. Properly stored, they stay fresh for 1–2 weeks. Remove any spoiled berries to prevent the rest from deteriorating.

content.title: About
content.content: Bouillabaisse is a traditional Provençal fish stew made with several types of seafood, fish, shellfish, tomatoes, saffron and aromatic herbs. Served hot, often accompanied by croutons and rouille.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bouillabaisse originated in the port of Marseille, where fishermen used unsold catch to make a flavorful broth.
The classic recipe calls for at least three fish species: sea bass, rascasse, and conger eel.
Saffron, which gives the dish its golden hue, was historically an expensive spice, so it was used sparingly.
Marseille hosts an annual "Bouillabaisse Competition" where judges evaluate aroma, taste and presentation.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fish and shellfish provide EPA and DHA, supporting heart and brain health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: The stew supplies a complete set of essential amino acids for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cod, sea bass and shellfish are abundant in B12 and niacin, important for nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: iodine, zinc, selenium
items.content: Seafood is a good source of trace elements that boost immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from tomatoes and saffron
items.content: Lycopene in tomatoes and crocin in saffron help combat free radicals.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to fish or shellfish.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Bouillabaisse often contains added salt and fish sauce, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly cooked shellfish can harbor toxins; always use fresh ingredients and cook thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot in a deep bowl, often with toasted croutons topped with rouille (garlic‑saffron mayo) and a sprinkle of fresh parsley. A squeeze of lemon brightens the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat to a rolling boil to ensure safety.
